strengths: Substantial and well-motivated corpus contribution: 14,538 training and 1,169 held-out evaluation instances with explicit thought-action-observation traces (~100K reasoning steps) spanning GIS operations, spectral indices (NDVI/NBR/NDBI), RGB/SAR imagery, and change detection — a gap clearly identified relative to perception-only EO VLMs (GeoChat, EarthDial) and domain-agnostic agents (OpenThinkIMG, OctoTools).

Carefully documented data-curation pipeline (Fig. 2) with automated validation: programmatic execution of candidate GIS queries, deterministic replay of trajectories before training, and manual inspection of test samples; the unified JSON schema and tool registry (Table A2) are described in enough detail to support reproducibility.

Broad and honest baseline coverage: 10 models from frontier (GPT-4o, o4-mini) to small open-weight models under both step-by-step and end-to-end protocols, with complementary metrics (tool/argument accuracy, F1 per functional category, tool-order fidelity under three constraint levels).

Useful supplementary analyses: backbone ablation (Qwen3-4B vs Qwen2.5-7B), error-taxonomy analysis (Fig. A4), qualitative zero-shot examples (Figs. A1–A3), and the exact LLM-judge evaluation prompt, which improves transparency of the assessment protocol.

The paper is appropriately positioned as a framework/dataset contribution rather than an algorithmic advance, and the claims (tool-order fidelity, argument grounding) are supported by the specific metrics that test them (AnyOrder/SameOrder/Unique, ArgN/ArgV).
weaknesses: Self-benchmarking bias: OpenEarthAgent is fine-tuned on trajectories generated from the same templates, tool suite, and synthesis pipeline as the test set, so its large gains (e.g., ArgN 96.08 vs 85.48 for GPT-4o) partly measure familiarity with the benchmark format rather than generalizable geospatial reasoning. No out-of-distribution evaluation, no comparison against the closest related system (ThinkGeo), and no fine-tuning of any baseline on the corpus to disentangle schema familiarity from spatial reasoning ability.

Answer accuracy relies on an LLM judge (gpt-4o-mini) with only qualitative description of scoring; there is no human-agreement validation of the judge, and numerical tolerance (±10%) and semantic-equivalence criteria could systematically favor models whose answer style matches the synthetic ground truths.

Evaluation-protocol details are loose: the first reasoning step is exempt from validation (why and with what effect on Inst. scores is unclear), the maximum number of end-to-end steps is unspecified despite being decisive for the reported 94–98% incomplete-execution failures of Llama/Mistral, and instance-level accuracy metrics overlap heavily (Inst./Tool/ArgN), making some rows redundant.

Presentation errors undermine polish: a broken cross-reference ('Table ??') on page 5, a duplicated clause ('and a batch size of 16.') on page 12, text quoting 'improving answer accuracy (45.26)' while Table 3 contains no such column (45.26 is the end-to-end Ans. value), a GSD mismatch (0.6 in Fig. A2 vs 0.072 in the accompanying text), and claimed 'state-of-the-art' despite GPT-4o retaining the lead on Summ., Op. F1, and Gen. accuracy.

The formalism in Sec. 4.2–4.3 (Eqs. 1–3) restates standard SFT with response masking and adds little methodological novelty; the framework is essentially OpenThinkIMG-style tool orchestration instantiated for EO, so the contribution rests almost entirely on data quality — yet no inter-annotator/LLM-consistency checks of the synthesized reasoning traces are reported.

Potential conflicts of interest are not addressed: the cited works ThinkGeo, EarthDial, TerraFM, and Geo-OLM share overlapping authorship with this submission, and no data/code release commitment is stated, which affects both attribution and reproducibility.

Missing limitations/societal-impact discussion: geospatial agent errors can propagate to disaster-response or monitoring decisions; the paper never quantifies failure severity on physically grounded outputs (e.g., wrong GSD scaling producing wrong distances), only error counts.

strengths: Timely and practically relevant problem: tool-augmented, multi-step reasoning for earth observation (GIS operations, spectral indices, SAR/optical) addresses a genuine gap between perception-centric RS VLMs and agentic frameworks.

Substantial curation effort: a corpus of 14,538 training / 1,169 evaluation instances spanning multiple modalities and seven thematic domains, with an automated validation pipeline (programmatic tool-call execution, deterministic replay of trajectories) that improves the credibility of the supervision data.

Well-organized unified tool registry (Section 4.2, Table A2) with standardized JSON contracts, execution caching, and extensibility; the trajectory formalization in Section 4.3 with observation masking from the loss is clean and sensible.

Large gains over the identical-size base model (Qwen3-4B: 33.55 → 62.10 ArgV; 13.72 → 45.26 Ans. accuracy in Table 4) and balanced category-wise F1, supporting the claim that SFT on verified trajectories improves structured tool use.

Reasonable evaluation design in places: two protocols (step-by-step and end-to-end), tool-order fidelity metrics under increasing constraints, and a supplementary error taxonomy (Fig. A4) that adds interpretability.
weaknesses: The evaluation is largely self-referential: the benchmark is the authors' own held-out split, generated by the same LLM-driven synthesis pipeline as the training data, and final-answer accuracy is judged by an LLM (gpt-4o-mini). This creates a distribution-matching advantage for the fine-tuned model and makes the headline numbers hard to interpret as genuine generalization; no external benchmark (e.g., ThinkGeo's suite) is used despite being closely related work.

The most relevant prior systems (ThinkGeo, Earth-Agent, Geo-OLM) are discussed extensively and compared only qualitatively via a self-serving feature checklist (Table 1), never empirically. Claiming a 'unified framework' contribution without running these baselines substantially weakens the experimental case.

Provenance of the reasoning traces is underspecified: the LLM used to synthesize queries and trajectories, prompt templates, and the fraction of manually verified samples are not reported. If traces are distilled from a frontier model, the paper is essentially distillation into a 4B model, and this framing/limitation should be explicit.

No meaningful ablations: no analysis of data scale, trajectory length, tool diversity, or the effect of the validation/replay filtering. The only 'ablation' (Table A1) is a backbone selection on 25% of the data and reports near-saturated F1 (96–99), suggesting metrics are too easy and limiting diagnostic value.

Potential train/test leakage concerns: training and evaluation samples derive from the same source datasets (e.g., DOTA, xBD), the same GEE regions, and the same query templates; geographic or template-level de-duplication is not described.

Presentation and rigor issues: a broken reference ('see Table ??'), a duplicated sentence ('and a batch size of 16. and a batch size of 16.'), unspecified max-step budgets and decoding settings for the end-to-end protocol, and missing details on how Summ./Ans. tolerance thresholds were validated. These suggest the manuscript is not yet polished to venue standards.

Answer accuracy remains modest overall (45.26 end-to-end), and index-task evaluation relies on a narrow set of three indices (NDVI/NBR/NDBI), limiting the breadth claim. No statement on public release of data, code, or the benchmark is given, which for a dataset/benchmark-flavored contribution is a significant reproducibility gap.
No limitations or societal-impact discussion, which is notable for a remote-sensing system aimed at disaster response and environmental monitoring applications.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: the paper unifies tool-augmented reasoning with GIS/spectral EO analysis, going beyond perception-centric RS VLMs (GeoChat, EarthDial) and geospatially naive agentic systems (OpenThinkIMG, OctoTools). Table 1 provides a useful positioning against related agent frameworks.

Substantial corpus contribution appropriate to a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution: 14,538 training and 1,169 held-out evaluation instances with ~100K reasoning steps, spanning GIS operations, spectral indices (NDVI/NBR/NDBI), change detection, and RGB/SAR imagery, drawn from well-established sources (DOTA, DIOR, xBD, SSDD, OpenStreetMap, GEE).

Thoughtful data-curation pipeline (Fig. 2) with automated validation: tool calls are programmatically replayed to verify argument correctness, geometric validity, and spatial consistency before training; test samples additionally receive manual inspection. This verification-before-training design is a concrete strength.
Well-specified unified tool registry with standardized JSON contracts and a tool execution cache (Table A2), enabling extensibility without retraining and deterministic replay of trajectories.

Two complementary evaluation protocols (step-by-step tool-agnostic rollouts and end-to-end autonomous execution) with five metrics plus tool-order fidelity metrics, benchmarked against frontier models (GPT-4o, o4-mini) and multiple open-source baselines. The fine-tuned 4B model shows large gains over its base model and several 7B-8B baselines.

Supplementary material is substantive: backbone ablation (Qwen3-4B vs. Qwen2.5-7B under identical data), a four-category error taxonomy analysis, qualitative zero-shot traces, and a fully disclosed evaluation prompt, which supports reproducibility of the LLM-judge protocol.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to the authors' own benchmark, and OpenEarthAgent is trained on trajectories from the same task distribution and pipeline. There is no external generalization test (e.g., on ThinkGeo's or Earth-Agent's tasks), so the central claim of 'competitive performance relative to recent models' risks distribution-matching advantage rather than transferable reasoning ability.

Answer accuracy for non-generation tasks relies on gpt-4o-mini as an LLM judge with ±10% tolerance and IoU thresholds, while gpt-4o is itself a head-to-head competitor. No human agreement study or inter-judge validation is reported, creating potential circularity/bias concerns that are not addressed.

Methodological novelty is limited: the training recipe is standard supervised fine-tuning with response-only masking on distilled trajectories (Eq. 3). No RL or preference-based stage, no data-scaling or trajectory-quality ablations, and no comparison against simply prompting a strong base model with the same tool registry to isolate the effect of fine-tuning versus in-context tool schemas.

Technical clarity gaps around multimodality: the base model is stated as Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (a text-instruct model), yet the agent consumes RGB, SAR, GeoTIFF, and index imagery. The vision encoder, image tokenization, and handling of multispectral/georeferenced rasters (beyond 3-channel RGB) are never described. How 'SAR-based reasoning' actually operates is unclear.

Presentation issues undermine polish: a broken cross-reference ('see Table ??' in Sec. 3), a duplicated sentence ('and a batch size of 16. and a batch size of 16.' in Sec. 5.1), an internally inconsistent GSD unit (0.6 px/meter in Fig. A2, which should presumably be m/px), and Fig. A3 shows a leftover 'malls.' fragment in the reasoning text. These suggest insufficient proofreading for a submission of this scope.

Self-serving comparison table (Table 1) lists binary checkmarks without qualification, e.g., marking change detection as covered when the traces suggest text-driven ChangeDetection tool calls rather than dedicated change-analysis capability; relative weaknesses of prior work are asserted rather than demonstrated.

Reproducibility and provenance are underspecified: no explicit statement that the dataset, code, or trained model will be released; licensing and redistribution terms for the aggregated source datasets are not discussed; the human verification effort (who, how many annotators, agreement rates) is not quantified.

No limitations or societal-impact discussion is provided. For a geospatial agent intended for disaster response and environmental monitoring, discussing failure modes (e.g., hallucinated POIs, geocoding errors as in Fig. 1, GSD-induced area miscalculations) and misuse risks would be expected.

Some claims overstate results: OpenEarthAgent still trails GPT-4o on generation accuracy (75.86 vs. 77.93) and its Summ. accuracy (83.64) is roughly at parity with the much smaller-parameter baseline's base capability; the paper's narrative of 'state-of-the-art' should be tempered to domain-specific tool-use metrics.

strengths: Substantial and diverse corpus: 14,538 training and 1,169 evaluation instances spanning optical, SAR, GIS, and index-based modalities, drawn from many well-established EO datasets (DOTA, DIOR, xBD, FloodNet, SSDD, etc.), with a clearly documented data-construction pipeline including programmatic execution checks and manual verification of the test set.

Deterministic replay validation of reasoning trajectories is a sensible and concrete mechanism for ensuring executability and spatial/ logical consistency of training traces, and the masked-loss training formulation is cleanly specified.

Evaluation is notably thorough for a benchmark paper: step-by-step and end-to-end protocols, trajectory-level tool-order fidelity metrics, error taxonomy, domain-stratified breakdowns, comparison against frontier and open baselines, cross-benchmark evaluation on Earth-Agent, and ablations on data composition, in-context learning, tool schema exposure, tool ordering, and high-level planning.

The LLM-judge robustness check (swapping gpt-4o-mini for Qwen3-30B while preserving rankings) and the released evaluation prompt improve the credibility and reproducibility of the Answer Accuracy metric.
The demonstration that a 4B fine-tuned model reaches near-frontier tool-usage fidelity (Table 3) and that ICL alone (k up to 15) does not close the gap (Table A2) is an informative empirical finding.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily data engineering plus supervised fine-tuning rather than a new method; the paper would benefit from being more explicit that this is a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, as the algorithmic novelty (tool registry, ReAct-style trajectories, SFT with loss masking) is limited relative to prior work (OpenThinkIMG, OctoTools, ThinkGeo, Earth-Agent).

Both the training data and the benchmark are synthesized by the same LLM pipeline with one exemplar per task category, creating a real risk that the benchmark rewards mimicry of the generator's trace style, phrasing, and tool-call templates rather than genuine geospatial reasoning. There is no human-authored or independently collected evaluation set to rule this out, and the very low open-source baseline scores (e.g., near-zero on some domains) are consistent with severe distribution shift rather than task difficulty.

The headline comparison is somewhat unfair by construction: OpenEarthAgent is fine-tuned on trajectories from exactly this distribution, tool registry, and schema, while all baselines (including GPT-5/o4-mini) are evaluated zero-shot or with ICL. The cross-benchmark result on Earth-Agent partially mitigates this, but tools were reformatted to conform to the OpenEarthAgent interface, again favoring the trained model.

The evaluation protocol itself has weaknesses: Answer Accuracy relies on an LLM judge with a generous ±10% numerical tolerance for spatial/area/distance quantities, which is permissive for geospatial measurements; the reported gain over GPT-5 (45.26 vs 43.88) is small and within plausible judge noise.

Summarization accuracy of OpenEarthAgent (83.64) is actually below o4-mini (89.48), and the final-answer accuracy remains modest in absolute terms; the paper frames tool-syntax metrics as state-of-the-art but these are heavily schema-shaped metrics.

No limitations or societal-impact discussion is provided in the main text, and while release is promised, neither code, data, nor models appear to be available at submission time, which complicates reproducibility of the benchmark.
Some claims in Table 1 (e.g., Earth-Agent lacking GIS and spectral coverage) appear to undersell the closest related work; the related-work positioning should be more carefully calibrated.
Missing details on geographic/spatial diversity and potential train-test leakage risk (same underlying scenes across splits) would strengthen confidence in generalization.

strengths: Substantial curation effort: the corpus (14,538 train / 1,169 eval instances, ~100K validated reasoning steps) integrates optical, SAR, GIS, and index-based (NDVI/NBR/NDBI) modalities from well-known public sources, filling a real gap between perception-centric EO datasets and agentic, tool-use-oriented benchmarks.

Deterministic replay validation of trajectories (re-executing tool calls to verify argument formatting, coordinate integrity, and full-chain executability) is a sensible and concrete quality-control mechanism that distinguishes the work from purely LLM-generated agent corpora.

The supplementary material is unusually thorough: ablations on data composition (easy/hard trajectories), in-context learning vs. fine-tuning, five levels of tool-schema exposure, tool ordering, and high-level planning, plus a cross-benchmark evaluation on the Earth-Agent benchmark and a judge-swap robustness check.
The unified tool registry with standardized JSON contracts and a cache-based orchestrator is a clean engineering contribution that supports extensibility without retraining.
Error analysis (S4) and domain-stratified results (S5) provide some transparency into failure modes rather than only reporting aggregate gains.
weaknesses: Circular / in-distribution evaluation bias: the test set is generated by the same pipeline, in the same tool schema, as the training data, and OpenEarthAgent is fine-tuned on exactly that schema (the schema ablation in Table A3 shows a massive gap between minimal and maximal schema exposure). Frontier baselines (GPT-5, o4-mini) are evaluated zero-shot without this conditioning, so the headline Inst./ArgN/ArgV advantages largely measure schema compliance that SFT directly optimizes, rather than superior geospatial reasoning.

The core end-task metric barely improves: Answer Accuracy is 45.26 vs. 43.88 for GPT-5 and 59.48 for o4-mini on generation. Most reported gains are on procedural metrics (tool selection, argument names/values, tool-order fidelity) that are near-tautological for a model SFT'd on validated reference trajectories from the same distribution.

Reasoning traces are synthesized by LLMs (Qwen/ChatGPT one-shot templates) and validated only for executability, not semantic correctness or reasoning quality; the risk of templated, shallow, or shortcut traces is not analyzed (e.g., no human audit or diversity statistics of queries beyond category counts).

Reliance on LLM-as-judge (gpt-4o-mini) for all non-generation answers; the judge-swap study shows a systematic positive bias with Qwen3-30B, but no human agreement study is provided to validate the judge protocol itself.

Domain-stratified results reveal weak generalization: accuracy drops to ~11.9 on aviation/transportation and ~23 on disaster assessment, and Logic F1 remains low (35.16) even on hard data, suggesting the model largely learns format adherence rather than robust spatial reasoning; this tempers the framing of 'geographically grounded' reasoning.

The methodological novelty is limited: trajectory SFT with a tool registry and ReAct-style traces is well-established (OpenThinkIMG, OctoTools, WebAgent, etc.); the paper's claim of novelty rests mainly on the dataset, so dataset quality and evaluation rigor are decisive, and both have the issues above.

Reproducibility is only promised ('code and models will be publicly available'); no license discussion for the aggregated imagery/annotations, and key construction details (LLM used for synthesis, exact prompt templates, deduplication, geographic coverage) are underspecified.

Presentation issues: Eq. (1) is a trivial restatement of a tool signature, several figures (Figs. 1, 3, 6, 7) are dense and hard to read, and the baseline claim that 'all models serve as interchangeable backbones' is not actually demonstrated for the frontier models.

strengths: Substantial and well-motivated resource: the corpus of 14,538 training and 1,169 evaluation instances with explicit, tool-grounded reasoning traces over optical, SAR, GIS, and spectral-index modalities fills a genuine gap between perception-centric EO datasets and agentic reasoning benchmarks, and is appropriately framed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution with a supporting framework.

The deterministic replay validation of trajectories before training (verifying argument formatting, coordinate integrity, geometric validity, and full-chain executability) is a concrete quality-control mechanism that lends credibility to the supervision data, and the unified tool registry with standardized JSON contracts is a clean, extensible design.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: step-by-step and end-to-end protocols, tool-selection F1 across functional categories, trajectory-order metrics (AnyOrder/SameOrder/Unique), tool-call success rates, domain-stratified breakdowns, error taxonomy, comparison against frontier (GPT-5, o4-mini) and open models, plus cross-benchmark evaluation on Earth-Agent.

The supplementary ablations are genuinely informative rather than decorative: data composition (easy/hard trajectories), tool-schema exposure levels, tool-list ordering, high-level planning, in-context learning scaling (k=5/10/15), and backbone selection (Qwen3-4B vs Qwen2.5-7B) each isolate a design decision and are well analyzed.

The ICL ablation (Table A2) partially addresses the fine-tuned-vs-prompted comparison concern by showing that even heavily prompted baselines remain well below the fine-tuned agent, supporting the claim that architectural/training-level adaptation matters.
Judge robustness is checked by substituting an open-source judge (Qwen3-30B) and confirming preserved rankings, which mitigates some concern about LLM-judged answer accuracy.
The paper is clearly written, with good figures, transparent dataset statistics, a documented tool inventory, and a released evaluation prompt, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Potential circularity between data construction and evaluation: both training traces and test instances are generated by the same LLM-driven pipeline (GPT-based question synthesizer and trace generator). The fine-tuned model is thus evaluated on data drawn from the same distribution it was trained on, while prompted baselines are not. This likely inflates OpenEarthAgent's advantage on tool-schema and trajectory metrics; the cross-benchmark result (Table A6) helps but the gap narrows substantially there.

Reference trajectories are treated as ground truth for tool-order metrics, yet many EO tasks admit multiple valid solution paths; the paper does not discuss how penalizing alternative-but-valid trajectories was avoided, which affects SameOrder/Unique and Tool accuracy interpretation.

Comparison fairness: baselines are zero-/few-shot prompted models with heterogeneous native tool-calling abilities; only the proposed model is fine-tuned on in-distribution data. A stronger control (e.g., SFT of a baseline backbone on generic tool data, or a non-geo agentic SFT baseline) is absent.

The SFT-only training objective on GPT-synthesized traces is essentially distillation; the paper does not probe whether the agent generalizes beyond template-style queries, real user phrasing, or unseen tool compositions, and no out-of-distribution (novel region/sensor/tool) test is reported.

Several metric details are underspecified: how Summary accuracy is scored for trajectories with non-unique valid answers, how numeric-tolerance thresholds (±10%) were chosen, and how image-generation 'success' is judged; given these metrics drive the headline claims, more precision is needed.

OpenEarthAgent trails frontier models on final answer quality (Summ. 83.64 vs 89.48 for o4-mini; Gen. 75.86 vs 77.93), so the 'near-frontier' narrative should be more carefully qualified; the wins are concentrated on schema adherence rather than answer correctness.

Attribution/novelty positioning: the components (ReAct-style traces, tool registry, SFT, replay validation) are established techniques; the contribution is their assembly for EO. This is acceptable for a benchmark paper, but the framework's technical novelty is modest and should not be oversold.

No discussion of dataset licensing/redistribution terms for the aggregated sources or of computational cost of replay validation; societal-impact considerations (e.g., misuse of fine-grained geospatial analysis) are not addressed.
